# Abstract

The Greater Indus basin (1,62M km², encompassing 1.621.984 km² and 21.951 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) supported the most aerially expansive urban culture of the Old World Bronze Age. Stretching from the Makran coast of Balochistan and the piedmont margins of the Sulaiman and Kirthar ranges to the alluvial plains of Punjab, the Ghaggar-Hakra palaeochannel system, the fertile silts of lower Sindh and the maritime littoral of Gujarat, the Indus Valley Civilisation developed an integrated network of orthogonal cities, walled port towns and rural farming hamlets. These societies combined winter cereals and summer millets with intensive animal husbandry and long-distance trade, sustaining demographic densities across arid and semi-arid riverine tracts that had previously supported only mobile pastoralists and localised forager bands.

Reconstructed across five physiographic and hydrological divisions from 10000BC to 1300BC under INDUS, regional population expanded from 140k terminal Pleistocene foragers in 10000BC during initial post-glacial recolonisation to 210k in 8000BC and 380k in 6000BC as aceramic and ceramic Neolithic farming villages coalesced at sites such as Mehrgarh on the Bolan River. Growth quickened through the fourth millennium BC as regional chalcolithic cultures developed, reaching 820k in 4000BC and 1,75M by 3000BC. During the Early to Mature Harappan transition, population expanded to 3,4M in 2500BC, reaching an all-time climactic apex of 4,5M inhabitants at 2200BC (yielding an aggregate regional density of 277,44 persons per 100 km²). Following the onset of regional hydroclimatic aridification associated with the 4,2ka BP event and shifting monsoon trajectories, nucleated cities underwent architectural degradation and demographic thinning, with regional population receding to 3,8M in 1900BC, 2,9M in 1500BC and 2,7M by 1300BC.

Demographic mass remained heavily concentrated along the principal alluvial channels and dry-river interfluves. At the 2200BC apex, Punjab, Cholistan and the Upper Indus-Gomal Basin accommodated 1,26M people (28% of regional population; 345,29 persons per 100 km²), anchored by Harappa and Ganweriwala [@Kenoyer1998AncientCities]. The Sindh and Lower Indus alluvial plain accommodated 1,08M inhabitants (24%; attaining the highest sub-regional density at 771,92 persons per 100 km²), centred on Mohenjo-daro and Chanhudaro [@Possehl1999IndusAge]. The Ghaggar-Hakra interfluve and Haryana supported 990k people (22%; 403,89 persons per 100 km²), anchored by Rakhigarhi and Banawali. The maritime province of Saurashtra, Kachchh and the Rajasthan Aravalli margin housed 720k people (16%; 136,13 persons per 100 km²), supported by Dholavira, Kalibangan and Lothal. The arid Balochistan highlands and Makran coast supported 450k inhabitants (10%; 131,14 persons per 100 km²).

This historical demographic synthesis combines 2.359 catalogued settlement trajectories with systematic multi-temporal remote sensing of archaeological mounds, geoarchaeological coring of palaeochannels and isotopic mobility analyses. By subtracting nucleated urban centres from dasymetrically distributed rural cultivators, the reconstruction captures the genuine balance between civil planning and rural agricultural resilience. The trajectory demonstrates that de-urbanisation after 2200BC was not a catastrophic demographic extinction, but an adaptive geographic devolution toward small rural communities in the eastern sub-Himalayan plains.

# Background

## Fluvial Ecology and Environmental Gradients

The ecological architecture of northwestern South Asia is governed by profound contrasts in topography, drainage dynamics and seasonal precipitation regimes [@Petrie2017Adaptation; @Neogi2019Geoarchaeo]. The Indus River trunk stream, fed by Karakoram and Himalayan snowmelt alongside monsoon runoff, flows across thousands of kilometres of gentle alluvial gradient, carrying high sediment loads that deposit fertile silts during annual summer inundations. Five major eastern tributaries - the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej - dissect the Punjab plain into distinct interfluvial zones (doabs), providing fertile ribbons of self-renewing alluvium flanked by higher, drier scrub plains [@GarciaMolsosa2023Reconstruc].

East of the Indus system lies the fossil drainage basin of the Ghaggar-Hakra, an ephemeral river network fed by seasonal monsoon rains along the Siwalik hills [@Orengo2017Large]. During the early and middle Holocene, this river corridor sustained continuous ribbons of dense settlement across Cholistan and Rajasthan, acting as an agrarian artery comparable to the main Indus stem. West of the Indus alluvium, the rugged limestone ridges of the Sulaiman and Kirthar ranges frame the Balochistan plateau. Here, perennial wadis and alluvial fans at the debouchment of mountain defiles, notably the Bolan and Gomal passes, created concentrated oasis environments capable of supporting early settled life [@Khan2021Hydro; @Lemmen2013Simulation].

To the southeast, the maritime littoral of Gujarat presents a contrasting ecological setting. During the third millennium BC, higher sea levels transformed the Great and Little Rann of Kachchh into navigable marine embayments, positioning island fortifications such as Dholavira at strategic points along coastal navigation lanes connecting the Persian Gulf with peninsular India [@Baba2018Developmen; @Fluckiger2024Dawn]. Seasonal monsoon precipitation decreases sharply from east to west, transitioning from over 800 mm annually in eastern Haryana to under 150 mm in the lower Indus valley and the Makran coast, rendering canal diversion, seasonal ponding and soil moisture conservation indispensable for sedentary food production [@Baba2018Developmen].

## Early Holocene Sedentism and the Neolithic Transition

The transition from foraging to food production in northwestern South Asia was rooted in the fertile piedmont fans of eastern Balochistan [@Lemmen2013Simulation; @Singh2023Subsistenc]. At Mehrgarh, situated along the Bolan River on the Kachi Plain, stratified excavations revealed continuous habitation spanning from the aceramic Neolithic (ca. 7000BC) through the chalcolithic era (ca. 2600BC) [@Khan2021Hydro]. Early levels document the local domestication of zebu cattle (*Bos indicus*), alongside the management of six-row naked barley (*Hordeum vulgare*), einkorn and emmer wheat [@Singh2023Subsistenc]. Mud-brick architecture with compartmentalised granaries appeared by 6000BC, accompanied by specialised pyrotechnology, bone tools and personal ornaments incorporating turquoise, lapis lazuli and marine shell.

Between 4000BC and 2600BC, sedentary village adaptations expanded from the highland piedmont into the broader floodplains of the Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra systems [@Petrie2019Chapter; @Bhavani2026Recent]. Distinct regional ceramic traditions developed during this Early Harappan epoch:
1. The Kot Diji tradition across central and northern Sindh, featuring wheel-turned globular jars with fish-scale motifs and early fortified citadel platforms.
2. The Amri tradition across lower Sindh, characterised by fine bichrome geometric pottery and riverbank hamlets.
3. The Sothi-Siswal horizon along the Ghaggar-Hakra drainage and Haryana, marked by incised and polychrome wares.
4. The Hakra ware complex in the Cholistan desert, reflecting dense concentrations of semi-permanent pastoralist encampments and craft villages.

These Early Harappan cultures laid the technological, social and ideological foundations for regional integration. Standardised mud-brick dimensions, fortified village perimeters, copper metallurgy and early proto-Indus script signs emerged across these disparate regions centuries prior to the Mature Harappan climax [@Wells1998Introducti; @Green2006State].

## Mature Harappan Urbanism and Civil Planning

Between 2600BC and 1900BC, northwestern South Asia witnessed the emergence of the Mature Harappan urban phenomenon, characterised by unprecedented regional standardisation across a territory exceeding one million square kilometres [@Petrie2019Chapter; @Sing2026Spatio]. Unlike contemporary Bronze Age cities in Mesopotamia and Egypt, Harappan urban centres were distinguished by sophisticated civic infrastructure rather than monumental royal palaces or dynastic mortuary temples [@Green2006State; @Shafaq2026Family].

The hallmarks of Mature Harappan urban planning encompassed:
- Modular brick architecture adhering strictly to a standard dimensional ratio of 1:2:4 (typically 7 by 14 by 28 cm for domestic walls and 10 by 20 by 40 cm for city perimeters), produced from kiln-fired clay in alluvial areas and dressed stone in rocky provinces such as Gujarat [@Khan2013Bricks].
- Bipartite and tripartite civic organisation, separating raised western citadels (equipped with civic baths, granaries and assembly halls) from expansive eastern lower towns organised along orthogonal street grids [@Green2006State].
- Advanced hydraulic engineering, including private courtyard wells, paved bathing platforms, covered terracotta-pipe sewage conduits discharging into exterior soakage jars and street-level drainage culverts [@Baba2018Developmen; @Khan2021Hydro].
- Specialised industrial districts dedicated to high-temperature pyrotechnology, including steatite seal engraving, micro-bead production, faience manufacture, chert blade knapping and copper-bronze alloying [@Parikh2019Inheritors; @Jain2026Layers].
- Standardised metrology, anchored by cubical chert weights following a binary-decimal ratio system, utilised uniformly from the Makran coast to western Uttar Pradesh [@Fluckiger2024Dawn].

At Mohenjo-daro in Sindh, the urban citadel featured the Great Bath, an engineered bitumen-lined hydraulic installation, alongside multi-roomed residential blocks served by over 700 municipal wells [@Khan2021Hydro]. At Dholavira on Khadir Island in the Rann of Kachchh, builders excavated monumental stone-lined reservoirs capable of storing hundreds of thousands of litres of seasonal storm runoff, insulating the city against desert drought [@Baba2018Developmen]. At Lothal on the Gulf of Khambhat, a massive brick-lined tidal basin operated as a maritime sluice dock, facilitating trade in carnelian, shell and bronze [@Fluckiger2024Dawn; @Kennedy2012Were].

## The 4,2ka BP Climatic Pulse and Post-Urban Transformation

Around 2200BC, a major global hydroclimatic reorganisation, the 4,2ka BP event, disrupted monsoon circulation across Afro-Eurasia [@Sarkar2016Oxygen; @Niederman2021Hydroclima]. Oxygen isotope profiles derived from Himalayan speleothems and archaeological bioapatites demonstrate a persistent multi-century weakening of the Indian summer monsoon and a reduction in winter cyclonic rainfall across northwestern India [@Sarkar2016Oxygen; @Niederman2021Hydroclima; @Jha2025Geoarchaeo]. Concurrently, tectonic shifts and sediment avulsion altered river courses; the Ghaggar-Hakra streamflow diminished as glacial headwaters diverted eastward into the Yamuna and westward into the Sutlej, leaving Cholistan river channels dry [@Orengo2017Large; @Neogi2019Geoarchaeo].

The demographic consequences of this drying phase unfolded over several centuries (2200BC to 1900BC) [@Petrie2019Revisiting; @Angourakis2020Downsize]. Cities reliant on massive surplus extraction and hydraulic maintenance suffered progressive structural collapse. Public sanitation systems ceased functioning, large residential compounds were subdivided into smaller tenements, kiln-fired brick manufacture waned in favour of scavenged mud-brick and long-distance trade in exotic prestige materials terminated [@Khan2013Bricks; @Shafaq2026Family].

By 1900BC, the Mature Harappan urban order gave way to regionalised Late Harappan horizons:
1. The Cemetery H complex in Punjab, characterised by red pottery with black painted mythological scenes and secondary urn burials [@Petrie2019Revisiting].
2. The Jhukar phase in Sindh, marked by rustic hand-made wares and squatter occupation atop decaying Mature Harappan brick mounds [@Petrie2019Chapter].
3. The Lustrous Red Ware and Rangpur phases in Gujarat, reflecting adaptation to seasonal millet farming [@Singh2023Subsistenc].
4. An eastward shift of rural settlements into the fertile, rain-fed sub-Himalayan valleys of Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, where agricultural communities adopted double-cropping of rice and millets [@Fuller2011Pathways; @Petrie2016Feeding; @Kumar2023Second].

Bioarchaeological investigations of human remains from late urban strata at Harappa and Rakhigarhi document heightened rates of cranial trauma, nutritional stress and infectious diseases such as leprosy and tuberculosis [@Anonymous2023Perspectiv; @Sachan2026Interperso]. These findings confirm that de-urbanisation was accompanied by social friction and interpersonal hardship among marginalised urban residents before populations dispersed into rural farming networks.

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Environmental Covariates

To reconstruct demographic densities across 1.621.984 km² of terrestrial surface, the INDUS spatial engine partitions the Greater Indus basin into 21.951 active 5-arcminute grid cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental covariates:
- Fluvial distance decay: proximity to perennial rivers (the Indus stem and the five Punjab rivers) and documented palaeochannels (Ghaggar-Hakra system), with exponential density attenuation beyond 15 km in arid tracts [@Orengo2017Large; @Neogi2019Geoarchaeo].
- Floodplain geomasking: binary and continuous weighting identifying active alluvium, silt-renewed terraces and seasonal mudflats capable of supporting inundation agriculture.
- Topographic slope: penalising rugged mountain slopes in the Sulaiman, Kirthar and Salt ranges while favouring flat alluvial plains, deltaic fan bluffs and coastal terraces.
- Bioclimatic suitability: incorporating palaeoclimatic moisture indices derived from regional speleothem and lake sediment records [@Sarkar2016Oxygen; @Niederman2021Hydroclima].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To eliminate double counting between nucleated urban centres and rural agricultural populations, 2.359 catalogued settlements with chronological population series are directly anchored to their WGS84 geographic coordinates. At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements inside each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The remaining rural population is then allocated across non-settled pixels in proportion to environmental suitability weights. A two-pass boundary feathering algorithm smoothes density transitions across sub-regional frontiers, preventing step discontinuities along mountain divides and administrative limits.

## Demographic Uncertainty Envelopes

Every sub-regional and macro-regional benchmark estimate carries an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 8% across all benchmark years from 10000BC to 1300BC). At the 2200BC apex, the regional total of 4,5M is bounded between 4,14M and 4,86M inhabitants. This uncertainty interval accommodates variances across competing archaeological house-size estimates, hearth-count multipliers and ceramic scatter boundaries [@Valentine2015Evidence; @Angourakis2020Downsize].

# Testing and Validation

## Remote Sensing and Archaeological Mound Detection

To validate settlement distributions against field archaeology, recent investigations have deployed machine learning classifiers on multisensor satellite imagery to automate archaeological tell detection [@Orengo2020Automated]. In the alluvial lowlands of Punjab, Sindh and Haryana, decades of river sedimentation and modern canal irrigation flattened subtle elevation gradients. By combining synthetic aperture radar (SAR), multispectral thermal emissions and multitemporal vegetation indices, Orengo and colleagues identified hundreds of previously unrecorded settlement mounds exhibiting distinct moisture retention signatures and anthropogenic soil coloration [@Orengo2020Automated; @Orengo2017Large].

These remote sensing surveys demonstrate that ancient settlement density was substantially higher than indicated by twentieth-century vehicular surface surveys [@GarciaMolsosa2023Reconstruc]. Furthermore, historical map analysis utilising late nineteenth-century Survey of India cartography and colonial gazetteers [@ImperialGazetteer1908] revealed ancient mound toponyms (*theh*, *tibba*, *deri*) that were subsequently erased by modern agricultural expansion, providing independent spatial ground-truthing for the 2.359 catalogued localities included in this study [@GarciaMolsosa2023Reconstruc].

## Bioarchaeological and Isotopic Verification

Excavations across Harappan necropolises provide biological constraints on demographic reconstructions [@Valentine2015Evidence; @Anonymous2023Perspectiv]. Lead ($^{206}\text{Pb}/^{204}\text{Pb}$) and strontium ($^{87}\text{Sr}/^{86}\text{Sr}$) isotope analyses conducted by Valentine and colleagues on human dental enamel from Harappa revealed that a significant proportion of interred individuals spent their childhoods outside the Indus alluvium, in the crystalline highlands of Balochistan or peninsular India [@Valentine2015Evidence]. These isotopic data confirm that major cities functioned as cosmopolitan centres drawing sustained migration from surrounding pastoral and highland populations.

Oxygen isotope ratios ($\delta^{18}\text{O}$) preserved in archaeological bioapatites and freshwater gastropod shells from Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi and Kotla Dahar lake sediments record progressive aridification between 2500BC and 1900BC [@Sarkar2016Oxygen; @Niederman2021Hydroclima]. The alignment between isotopic drying pulses and regional settlement contraction validates the climatic forcing mechanisms incorporated into the INDUS demographic trajectory.

## Agricultural Multi-Cropping and Caloric Calibration

Archaeobotanical analyses from northwest India demonstrate that Harappan societies pioneered sophisticated multi-cropping agricultural regimes [@Fuller2011Pathways; @Petrie2016Feeding; @Singh2023Subsistenc]. Winter cropping (*rabi*) focused on wheat, barley, peas, chickpeas and mustard, planted in autumn to capture post-monsoon soil moisture and winter rains. Summer cropping (*kharif*) incorporated drought-tolerant small millets (*Setaria*, *Panicum*), tropical pulses (mung bean, black gram) and indigenous rice (*Oryza sativa*), sown with the arrival of the southwest monsoon [@Fuller2011Pathways; @Petrie2016Feeding].

This dual-season regime insulated agrarian communities against localised seasonal crop failures. When the summer monsoon faltered during the late third millennium BC, communities expanded their reliance on winter pulses and drought-resistant millets, facilitating the gradual reorientation of demographic mass toward the eastern margins of the basin rather than precipitating total systemic collapse [@Petrie2017Adaptation; @Angourakis2020Downsize].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The INDUS source ledger was compiled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process anchored in primary archaeological monographs [@Possehl1999IndusAge; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities; @Allchin1995Archaeology] and regional survey baselines [@ImperialGazetteer1908] to eliminate geographic omission biases:
- Wave 1: Programmatic ingestion of official national census baselines, primary-monograph imperial metropolis anchors and national heritage registries, yielding 1.368 georeferenced settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of site records from multi-repository archaeological and monument corpora (Pleiades, Zenodo Harappan, Vidarbha and Palaeolithic inventories, Archaeological Survey of India records, Wikidata, OpenStreetMap and radiocarbon databases), incorporating 661 settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill integrating macro-calibrated pre-1800 *qasba*, *pargana* and *nadu* settlement continuity [@Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade] alongside strict Bronze Age foundation-year and chronological toponymy audits, adding 330 early and peripheral sites.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps and GeoNames homonym audits across all five divisions, yielding zero unaccounted settlements and confirming asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 2.964 candidate localities were audited: 2.359 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements (712 in Punjab and Upper Indus, 669 in Ghaggar-Hakra and Haryana, 608 in Gujarat and Rajasthan, 199 in Sindh and Lower Indus, and 171 in Balochistan and Makran) and 605 were excluded as duplicate survey aliases within the spatial consolidation radius.

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The demographic history of the Greater Indus basin across nine millennia demonstrates a classic civilisational trajectory: prolonged Neolithic gestation, rapid Mature Harappan urbanisation, climactic population apex and post-urban rural devolution (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

## Four Historical Demographic Epochs

### Terminal Pleistocene and Early Holocene Foraging (10000BC to 6000BC)

During the terminal Pleistocene and early Holocene, northwestern South Asia was occupied by small, mobile forager bands exploiting riverine fisheries, piedmont gazelle herds and wild cereal grasses. Regional population stood at 140k in 10000BC (yielding an aggregate density of 0,86 persons per 100 km²), rising gradually to 210k in 8000BC and 380k by 6000BC (2,34 persons per 100 km²). Settlement was concentrated along perennial river confluences and highland springs in Balochistan, where rock shelters and seasonal camp sites provided access to diverse ecological zones [@Lemmen2013Simulation].

### Neolithic Transformation and Chalcolithic Emergence (6000BC to 3000BC)

Between 6000BC and 3000BC, the establishment of permanent mud-brick villages, cattle pastoralism and cereal cultivation triggered sustained demographic growth. Population reached 820k by 4000BC (5,06 persons per 100 km²) and more than doubled to 1,75M by 3000BC (10,79 persons per 100 km²). During this epoch, settlement expanded from the Balochistan piedmont into the fertile floodplains of the Indus, Gomal and Ghaggar-Hakra systems. Craft specialisation and regional ceramic spheres emerged, marking the transition from self-contained Neolithic hamlets to complex chalcolithic interaction networks [@Petrie2019Chapter; @Bhavani2026Recent].

### Mature Harappan Climax and Urban Integration (3000BC to 2200BC)

The centuries between 3000BC and 2200BC represented the most explosive phase of demographic and civic expansion in prehistoric South Asia [@Sing2026Spatio]. Regional population climbed from 1,75M in 3000BC to 3,4M in 2500BC, attaining an all-time peak of 4,5M inhabitants at 2200BC (yielding an aggregate density of 277,44 persons per 100 km²).

This urban climax was characterised by the rapid foundation and expansion of primary cities [@Kenoyer1998AncientCities; @Possehl1999IndusAge]:
- Mohenjo-daro in Sindh grew into a metropolis covering over 250 ha, supporting an estimated peak population of 42k inhabitants in 2200BC [@Khan2021Hydro; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities].
- Rakhigarhi in Haryana expanded across multiple mounds covering over 300 ha, housing 40k people in 2200BC and serving as the primary eastern regional capital [@Anonymous2023Perspectiv; @Possehl1999IndusAge].
- Harappa in Punjab covered over 150 ha with a peak urban population of 35k inhabitants in 2200BC, commanding trade along the Ravi River [@Petrie2019Chapter; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities].
- Ganweriwala in Cholistan occupied a strategic midpoint along the dry Hakra bed, housing 26k inhabitants in 2200BC [@Possehl1999IndusAge].
- Dholavira in Kachchh accommodated 20k inhabitants in 2200BC within monumental stone-faced fortifications, managing marine trade through the Rann [@Baba2018Developmen; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities].

By 2200BC, the five sub-regions attained their historic maximum densities: Sindh reached 771,92 persons per 100 km², Ghaggar-Hakra reached 403,89, Punjab reached 345,29, Gujarat reached 136,13 and Balochistan reached 131,14.

Inter-regional exchange sustained these massive demographic nucleations. Steatite seals carved with animal emblems and brief inscriptions acted as administrative property markers [@Wells1998Introducti; @Umer2026Religious]. Long-distance trade routes linked coastal ports with interior crafting towns:
- Marine gastropod shells (*Turbinella pyrum*) harvested along the Makran coast were shipped to Harappa and Lothal for bangle cutting [@Fluckiger2024Dawn].
- Raw carnelian and agate nodules from the Ratanpur mines in Gujarat were transported to Chanhudaro and Lothal for high-precision copper-drill perforation [@Parikh2019Inheritors; @Jain2026Layers].
- Lapis lazuli extracted from Badakhshan was routed through northern outposts such as Shortugai along the Oxus River, linking Central Asian mineral circuits with the Indus lowlands [@Fluckiger2024Dawn].
- Timber, copper ingots from the Khetri mines of Rajasthan and tin flowed into urban foundries, sustaining extensive bronze tooling and weapon manufacture.

### Post-Urban Reorganisation and Rural De-Concentration (2200BC to 1300BC)

Following the 2200BC peak, regional population contracted to 3,8M in 1900BC (-15,6% reduction over three centuries), declining further to 2,9M in 1500BC and 2,7M by 1300BC. Rather than reflecting sudden societal collapse, this transition witnessed the selective abandonment of large urban centres in Sindh and Cholistan in favour of smaller, dispersed agricultural settlements in eastern Punjab, Haryana and Gujarat [@Petrie2019Revisiting; @Angourakis2020Downsize]. In Gujarat and Haryana, settlement numbers actually increased during the Late Harappan period, though average site sizes shrank from tens of hectares to small hamlets of 1 to 3 ha [@Parikh2019Inheritors; @Singh2023Subsistenc].

The urban settlement hierarchy across the 2.359 catalogued settlements fits a Zipf rank-size power law with $\alpha = 0,87$ and $R^2 = 0,92$, conforming to a multi-tiered structural organisation [@Kenoyer1998AncientCities; @Possehl1999IndusAge]:
1. Primary metropolises (20k or more inhabitants): Mohenjo-daro (42k in 2200BC), Rakhigarhi (40k in 2200BC), Harappa (35k in 2200BC), Ganweriwala (26k in 2200BC) and Dholavira (20k in 2200BC). These centres coordinated regional craft production, civic administration and long-distance exchange.
2. Major regional centres (10k to 20k inhabitants): Rehman Dheri (13k peak in 2500BC, 11k in 2200BC) and Kalibangan (12,5k in 2200BC). These walled towns commanded key geographical gateways and river crossings.
3. Secondary specialised towns (5k to 10k inhabitants): Lothal (9,5k in 2200BC), Chanhudaro (8,5k in 2200BC), Banawali (8,5k in 2200BC), Kot Diji (7,5k peak in 2500BC, 6,5k in 2200BC), Gilund (6,5k in 2200BC), Farmana (6,5k in 2200BC), Bhirrana (6,5k peak in 2500BC, 6k in 2200BC), Amri (5,5k peak in 2500BC, 5k in 2200BC), Ahar (5,5k in 2200BC) and Rojdi (5k in 2200BC). These centres served as nodes for carnelian bead manufacturing, seal carving, metallurgy and shell working.
4. Tertiary agrarian towns, villages and outposts (under 5k inhabitants): Surkotada (4,2k in 2200BC), Balakot (4,2k in 2200BC), Mehrgarh (4,2k peak in 3000BC), Sutkagen Dor (3,2k in 2200BC) and over two thousand smaller rural farming settlements catalogued throughout the basin.

# Limitations

Archaeological visibility and demographic reconstruction in the Greater Indus basin remain subject to significant taphonomic and preservation biases:
1. Fluvial alluviation and river avulsion: the Indus and its tributaries are dynamic braided rivers that have shifted their channels repeatedly over millennia [@GarciaMolsosa2023Reconstruc; @Jha2025Geoarchaeo]. Early Holocene sites situated on ancient floodplain margins frequently lie buried beneath 5 to 8 metres of post-Bronze Age alluvium, while other settlements were obliterated by channel migration.
2. Anthropogenic destruction in modern times: during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, extensive railway construction dismantled ancient mud-brick mounds for track ballast, most notably at Harappa. Furthermore, deep mechanical ploughing and modern brick kilns across Punjab, Haryana and Sindh have levelled thousands of small rural sites [@GarciaMolsosa2023Reconstruc].
3. Differential geographic preservation: architectural remains in arid Sindh, Balochistan and Kachchh (such as baked bricks at Mohenjo-daro and dressed limestone at Dholavira) exhibit superior preservation compared to mud-brick structures in the humid monsoon belts of eastern Punjab and Haryana.
4. Script undecipherability: because the Indus script remains undeciphered, demographic reconstructions cannot draw upon contemporary administrative tax rolls, censuses or dynastic archives, requiring reliance upon excavated house footprints, room counts and settlement areas [@Wells1998Introducti; @Green2006State].

# Conclusion

The Indus Valley Civilisation established an unprecedented demographic concentration in Bronze Age South Asia, expanding from 140k terminal Pleistocene foragers in 10000BC to an all-time climactic apex of 4,5M inhabitants at 2200BC across 1,62M km² of territory. This demographic achievement was made possible by the integration of winter and summer multi-cropping, kiln-fired modular brick architecture, sophisticated municipal hydraulic systems and inter-regional exchange networks linking highland pastoralists with riverine farmers and coastal traders.

The de-urbanisation of the Indus civilisation following the 4,2ka BP climatic event was not a catastrophic population extinction, but an adaptive structural transition [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation]. As weakening monsoon rains and river migrations disrupted the intensive agricultural foundations of the central floodplains, urban public infrastructure dissolved and populations decentralised into rural farming villages in eastern Punjab, Haryana and Gujarat. This rural redistribution laid the demographic and technological foundations for the subsequent emergence of Iron Age societies in the Gangetic plain during the first millennium BC.
